This is news to me. Not challenging you, but could you share more about this? Why was this the catalyst? I thought the war started because they were ending slavery.

They weren't ending slavery specifically. It wasn't that Lincoln declared slavery illegal then there was a rebellion. Slavery was on the decline and many states outlawed it. In the declaration of secession, South Carolina (first state to secede) specifically laid out that northern states were failing to abide by the fugitive slave law by allowing fugitive slaves to run away/hide. Additionally, new states that were joining in the west were entering as free states, so the balance of power was shifting.

Slavery was on the decline, but it would've been an issue that was fought over in the congressional battleground for decades. The war accelerated it dramatically. That said, the Union had 5 slave states: Maryland, Missouri, Delaware, Kentucky, and West Virginia (though WV planned to end it when they split off from Virginia). The Union wasn't fighting against slavery (initially), they were fighting to keep the union together. The Emancipation Proclamation did not free all slaves; it only freed those slaves in the south (which meant bubkis since those states weren't under the US government). The 13th amendment ending slavery was passed in 1865, towards the end of the civil war, and the 14th amendment (rights are protected for all citizens) and 15th amendment (giving all citizens the right to vote) were largely fueled by reconstruction.

Further (at least according to one book I read), anti-racist sentiment among the northerners was partly fueled by the war. White soldiers for the union fought and died alongside black soldiers and there was a strong feeling in the North that the war was against slavery. When you fight next to a black guy and he saves your life, it's hard to go back after the war and think of him as less than human. It greatly accelerated equality in the north. Arguably, the years directly following the civil war had much less racism in the north than the early 1900s (especially 1910s-1920s; Wilson and his cabinet were huge racists and anti-black sentiment was a large part of the Democratic party platform from Reconstruction up through the Civil Rights Movement).

The war and reconstruction were huge steps forward in abolition and race relations. While we can't know what would have happened if South Carolina hasn't seceded, it would have been a much more drawn out process.
